objectives: Describe the long-term causes: alliances, militarism, imperial rivalry, nationalism
Explain the immediate cause and the outbreak of war

blocks.title: Long-term causes
blocks.md: **Alliances:** Europe divided into the Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) and the Triple Entente (France, Russia, Britain). **Militarism:** an arms race, especially in armies and navies. **Imperial rivalry:** competition for colonies and trade. **Nationalism:** pride, and the ambitions of national groups in the Balkans.

blocks.title: Outbreak
blocks.md: On **28 June 1914** Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, was assassinated in Sarajevo. Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia and declared war in late July. Alliances drew in Russia, Germany and France. When Germany invaded Belgium, Britain declared war on **4 August 1914**. The war ended with the armistice of **11 November 1918**.

blocks.caption: From Sarajevo to the Treaty of Versailles.
blocks.alt: Timeline with 1914 Sarajevo, 1916 partition of Kamerun, 1918 armistice, 1919 Versailles and the war period.

blocks.title: Africa in the war
blocks.md: Fighting took place in Africa because the powers’ colonies were also at war: in Togoland, Kamerun, German South West Africa and German East Africa. Africans served as soldiers and carriers and suffered requisitioning and hardship. The war ended German colonial rule in Africa, and the colonies were redistributed under League of Nations mandates.

blocks.title: Avoid these errors
blocks.md:
- The assassination was the trigger, not the only cause.
- Do not blame one country alone: historians debate the relative responsibility.
- Africa was not only a place of ‘sideshows’: its people and resources mattered to the war effort.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Trigger versus cause
blocks.statement: Explain the difference between the trigger and the long-term causes of the war.
steps: Long-term causes created tension: alliances, arms race, rivalry, nationalism.
The trigger was the assassination at Sarajevo in June 1914.
Without the tensions, the assassination might have remained a local crisis.
blocks.answer: Trigger sets off a war that long-term causes made possible.

blocks.title: Example 2 — How alliances widened the conflict
blocks.statement: Explain how alliances turned a local crisis into a general war.
steps: Russia supported Serbia, Germany supported Austria-Hungary.
France was allied to Russia, and Britain entered after the invasion of Belgium.
blocks.answer: Each alliance drew in further states.

lessons.title: The First World War in Kamerun and the partition
lessons.programRef: Cameroon GCE Board, Advanced Level History syllabus (Lower Sixth) — to be checked against the official text
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe the conquest of German Kamerun by the Allies (1914–16)
reviewNotes: Verify: Douala fell 27 September 1914 (commonly given); Mora surrender February 1916; Anglo-French partition 1916; ‘about four-fifths’ French share; mandates 1922; CDC created 1946.
Check the spelling ‘Cameroons’ (British) and ‘Cameroun’ (French) as used in the syllabus.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: The war in Kamerun
blocks.md: When war began in August 1914, British forces from Nigeria and French and Belgian forces from neighbouring colonies attacked German Kamerun. **Douala fell in September 1914**. German forces withdrew inland and into the interior; the last German strongholds, including Mora in the north, held out until **early 1916**. Many Germans and their African soldiers crossed into Spanish Guinea in early 1916.

blocks.title: Partition
blocks.md: In **1916** Britain and France agreed to divide Kamerun. France took the larger share, about four-fifths, in the east and south. Britain took two narrow strips along the border with Nigeria, **Northern and Southern Cameroons**, administered as part of Nigeria. The Treaty of Versailles (1919) took away Germany’s colonies, and in **1922** the League of Nations confirmed the division as mandates.

blocks.caption: From German to British and French administration.
blocks.alt: Timeline from 1884 to 1961 with German rule to 1916 then British and French rule, with 1914, 1916, 1922 and 1946.

blocks.title: Effects
blocks.md: The partition divided peoples and trade networks and left Cameroon under two administrative systems with different languages, laws and education. Plantations were taken over, and former German plantations in the British zone were later run by the Cameroons Development Corporation (CDC, set up in 1946). The war also brought deaths, forced labour and requisitions.

blocks.title: Frequent errors
blocks.md:
- Britain and France divided the territory; Germany did not hand it over by treaty in 1916.
- The mandate was confirmed in 1922, six years after the 1916 partition.
- Southern and Northern Cameroons were not one province but two separate strips administered with Nigeria.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Time between events
blocks.statement: Find the time from the fall of Douala (1914) to the confirmation of the mandate (1922).

blocks.title: Example 2 — Effect of partition
blocks.statement: Explain one long-term consequence of partitioning Kamerun between Britain and France.
steps: Two colonial systems introduced different languages, laws and schools.
These differences shaped the later political and social history of the territories.
Families and trade across the boundary were disrupted.
blocks.answer: Divergent administrative systems and divided communities.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Explain the consequences of the partition of Kamerun for the peoples of Cameroon.
exercises.model: Partition divided communities and trade networks along a new boundary. The French and British zones developed under different languages, laws, education and administrative systems, and the British zones were administered with Nigeria. These differences influenced later political questions about unification and identity. Economic life was also reorganised as plantations changed hands.
